💸 Social Giant To Pay $16.68 Billion For Designing Apps To Hook Teenagers; Calls It A 'Rounding Error With Feelings'

MENLO PARK — reported between two infinite scrolls

LEGAL — A social-media giant agreed to pay up to $16.68 billion to settle claims it deliberately engineered its apps to hook teenagers — a number large enough to sting slightly and small enough to be recouped by roughly Tuesday afternoon.

"We've always prioritized well-being," the company said, of platforms scientifically optimized to be impossible to put down, now paying a historic sum to acknowledge they succeeded. Analysts note the settlement confirms the apps were addictive by design, which everyone already knew — having checked the app in question about four times while reading this very sentence.

THE INTERNET — reported by a suddenly very quiet crowd

INDUSTRY — A tech giant is shutting down its long-running human-work marketplace after 21 years — the vast crowd of people who labeled the data and answered the questions that taught modern AI how to think — in what may be the most on-the-nose ending in tech history.

"We thank everyone for their contributions," the company said, closing the very service whose workers hand-fed the machine-learning era one tiny task at a time, until the machine no longer needed them. Historians will note that the tutors trained the pupil so well it graduated, took their job, and turned off the lights on the way out.

🔋 A.I. Company's Own Chip Beats The Chip King On Efficiency; The Customer Has Built A Better Toll Booth

SAN FRANCISCO — reported by the light of one very efficient LED

HARDWARE — A leading AI lab says its first custom inference chip now outperforms the dominant chipmaker's flagship systems on AI-work-per-watt — meaning the industry's biggest customer looked at the world's most expensive toll booth and decided to build its own road.

"We needed efficiency at our scale," the company said, of a chip born from the timeless frustration of paying someone else a fortune every single day. Analysts note that when your suppliers get rich enough, they eventually become your competitors — a lesson the chip king is now learning at a very high, very well-cooled clock speed.
